A dungeon is a dark, underground prison room or cell — typically found beneath a castle, fortress, or large stone building — where prisoners are held captive, often in terrible conditions.

Imagine a grand medieval castle. Most people think of castles as tall, impressive structures above the ground. But beneath them — dug into the earth, deep below the main floors — there are stone rooms sealed off from the outside world. These are dungeons.

They were built to hold people the king, lord, or ruler wanted locked away: captured enemies, criminals, political rivals, or anyone considered dangerous or inconvenient. Once you were thrown into a dungeon, escape was nearly impossible. The doors were heavy, the locks were strong, and the guards were right there.

The conditions inside a dungeon were deliberately harsh:

  • No natural light. Stone walls on all sides, no windows, and sometimes only a single torch or candle — or nothing at all.
  • Cold and damp. Being underground meant constant moisture seeping through the stone, making the air chilly and wet year-round.
  • Isolated. Prisoners were cut off from the world. Nobody could hear them scream. Nobody was coming to help.
  • Chained. Many prisoners were shackled to the walls or floor so they couldn't even move freely within the small space.
  • Bare minimum survival. Very little food, very little water, no comfort whatsoever.

This is why the word carries such a heavy, oppressive feeling. A dungeon is not just a prison — it is a deliberately miserable one.

In historical contexts, particularly in architecture and medieval history, "dungeon" was also used to refer to the main central tower of a castle — the strongest, most fortified part, sometimes called the "keep." This tower was where the lord resided and where defenders made their last stand during an attack.

Since this tower often had underground prison cells directly beneath it, people gradually began using the word "dungeon" to mean only the underground prison part, and the tower meaning faded away. You will almost never encounter this meaning in everyday modern English — it shows up mainly in history books and academic writing about medieval castles. When someone says "dungeon" today, they virtually always mean the underground prison.
In Fantasy, Gaming, and Popular Culture

In modern fantasy literature, films, and especially video games and tabletop role-playing games (most famously Dungeons & Dragons, often shortened to D&D), the word has expanded into something slightly different.

In these contexts, a "dungeon" refers to any dangerous underground complex — a network of tunnels, caves, corridors, or chambers — that a group of adventurers or heroes must explore. It is usually filled with monsters, deadly traps, puzzles, and hidden treasures. Here, a dungeon doesn't have to be a prison; it is simply a perilous underground world to navigate.

This gave rise to popular terms like:

  • Dungeon crawler — a style of game or story where characters explore dungeons room by room, fighting enemies and finding loot.
  • Dungeon crawling — the act of exploring such places.
  • Dungeon Master (DM) — in D&D, this is the person who controls and narrates the story, including the dungeon itself, for the other players.

People also use "dungeon" informally — and figuratively — to describe any real-world place that feels dark, gloomy, cramped, or suffocating, even if it isn't actually a prison or underground.

For example:

  • "My basement apartment feels like a dungeon — no light, no air."
  • "They kept the interns working in a dungeon of a back office."

The speaker isn't claiming it's a literal prison. They're using "dungeon" as a powerful, vivid word to say the place is depressingly dark and oppressive.
How It's Used in Sentences (Real Examples)

• The king ordered his enemy to be thrown into the dungeon.
  • After years in the dungeon, the prisoner had almost forgotten what sunlight looked like.
  • The video game sends players into a dungeon full of goblins and traps.
  • This apartment is tiny and dark — it's an absolute dungeon.

A dungeon is an underground prison of the darkest, most miserable kind — a place designed not just to hold someone, but to break them with isolation, darkness, cold, and hopelessness. From this core meaning, the word has branched out into fantasy and gaming to mean any dangerous underground labyrinth, and it is also used figuratively to describe any place that feels bleak and suffocating. Whichever way you encounter it, the word always carries that same core feeling: something underground, dark, inescapable, and deeply unpleasant.
